claim: NG2+ glia, also known as polydendrocytes or oligodendrocyte precursor cells, represent a new entity among glial cell populations in the central nervous system.
source: The NG2+ glia, also known as polydendrocytes or oligodendrocyte precursor cells, represent a new entity among glial cell populations in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a statement about the classification of NG2+ glia as a distinct glial cell type, drawing from established scientific knowledge about glial cell populations.

claim: The complete repertoire of roles for NG2+ glia is not yet identified.
source: However, the complete repertoire of their roles is not yet identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding NG2+ glia functions.

claim: Embryonic NG2+ glia originate from the Nkx2.1+ progenitors of the ventral telencephalon.
source: The embryonic NG2+ glia originate from the Nkx2.1+ progenitors of the ventral telencephalon.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using Nkx2.1-cre reporter mice showing YFP+ NG2+ glia in the dorsal telencephalon.

claim: Beginning from E12.5 until E16.5, NG2+ glia populate the entire dorsal telencephalon.
source: Our analysis unravels that, beginning from E12.5 until E16.5, the NG2+ glia populate the entire dorsal telencephalon.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing NG2+ glia distribution across developmental stages.

claim: The appearance of NG2+ glia temporally coincides with the establishment of blood vessel network in the embryonic brain.
source: Interestingly, their appearance temporally coincides with the establishment of blood vessel network in the embryonic brain.
evidence: This is based on observational data comparing the timing of NG2+ glia appearance with vessel network development.

claim: NG2+ glia are closely apposed to developing cerebral vessels by being either positioned at the sprouting tip cells or tethered along the vessel walls.
source: NG2+ glia are closely apposed to developing cerebral vessels by being either positioned at the sprouting tip cells or tethered along the vessel walls.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and confocal microscopy data showing spatial relationships between NG2+ glia and vessels.

claim: Absence of NG2+ glia drastically affects vascular development leading to severe reduction of ramifications and connections by E18.5.
source: Absence of NG2+ glia drastically affects the vascular development leading to severe reduction of ramifications and connections by E18.5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Nkx2.1-cre+/Rosa-DTA and Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-DTA mice showing vascular defects.

claim: Blood vessels develop by vasculogenesis, de novo synthesis involving differentiation of cells from endothelial precursor cells (angioblasts).
source: Blood vessels develop by two unique mechanisms: vasculogenesis, de novo synthesis involving differentiation of cells from endothelial precursor cells (angioblasts), and angiogenesis, formation of vessels from pre-existing vessels by either (a) sprouting, proliferation, and migration of endothelial cells (ECs) or (b) bifurcation of a preexisting blood vessel into two (Adams and Alitalo, 2007; Jain, 2003; Larrivee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on vascular development mechanisms.

claim: Blood vessels develop by angiogenesis, formation of vessels from pre-existing vessels by either sprouting, proliferation, and migration of endothelial cells or bifurcation of a preexisting blood vessel into two.
source: Blood vessels develop by two unique mechanisms: vasculogenesis, de novo synthesis involving differentiation of cells from endothelial precursor cells (angioblasts), and angiogenesis, formation of vessels from pre-existing vessels by either (a) sprouting, proliferation, and migration of endothelial cells (ECs) or (b) bifurcation of a preexisting blood vessel into two (Adams and Alitalo, 2007; Jain, 2003; Larrivee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on vascular development mechanisms.

claim: The selection of sprouting ECs is controlled positively by the pro-angiogenic vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
source: The selection of sprouting ECs is controlled positively by the pro-angiogenic vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and negatively by pericytes, extracellular matrix molecules or VEGF inhibitors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about VEGF's role in angiogenesis.

claim: The selection of sprouting ECs is controlled negatively by pericytes, extracellular matrix molecules or VEGF inhibitors.
source: The selection of sprouting ECs is controlled positively by the pro-angiogenic vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and negatively by pericytes, extracellular matrix molecules or VEGF inhibitors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about negative regulators of EC sprouting.

claim: Endothelial tip cells have the capacity to extend filopodia in order to respond to attractive or repulsive signals of the environment.
source: Thereafter, the endothelial tip cells have the capacity to extend filopodia in order to respond to attractive or repulsive signals of the environment.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about tip cell behavior during angiogenesis.

claim: Guidepost cells have been shown to direct tip cells pathfinding by cell contact adhesion or by secreting soluble guidance cues.
source: Guidepost cells have been shown to direct tip cells pathfinding by cell contact adhesion or by secreting soluble guidance cues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about guidepost cell functions in vascular development.

claim: Endothelial tip cells share numerous similarities with axonal growth cones.
source: Therefore, endothelial tip cells share numerous similarities with axonal growth cones and it is admitted that axons and blood vessels use similar mechanisms in order to form complex networks (Carmeliet and Tessier-Lavigne, 2005; Eichmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature comparing tip cells and growth cones.

claim: Axons and blood vessels use similar mechanisms in order to form complex networks.
source: Therefore, endothelial tip cells share numerous similarities with axonal growth cones and it is admitted that axons and blood vessels use similar mechanisms in order to form complex networks (Carmeliet and Tessier-Lavigne, 2005; Eichmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on shared mechanisms between neural and vascular development.

claim: Pathfinding of blood vessels has been shown to require Sema3E/PlexinD1, Netrin-1/Unc5B, and Slit/Robo4 signaling.
source: Additionally, pathfinding of blood vessels has been shown to require Sema3E/PlexinD1, Netrin-1/Unc5B, and Slit/Robo4 signaling (Adams and Alitalo, 2007; Carmeliet and Tessier-Lavigne, 2005; Lu et al., 2004; Larrivee et al., 2007; Eichmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on guidance signaling in vascular development.

claim: Blood vessels in the telencephalon of embryonic mice are divided into pial or periventricular vessels based on their anatomical location, their growth patterns and development.
source: Blood vessels in the telencephalon of embryonic mice are divided into pial or periventricular vessels based on their anatomical location, their growth patterns and development.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about vascular organization in the developing brain.

claim: The periventricular vessels are believed to give birth to the arterial networks.
source: The periventricular vessels are believed to give birth to the arterial networks, while the pial vessels may generate the venous sinuses (Hiruma et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on vessel development in the telencephalon.

claim: The pial vessels may generate the venous sinuses.
source: The periventricular vessels are believed to give birth to the arterial networks, while the pial vessels may generate the venous sinuses (Hiruma et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature and uses speculative language ('may').

claim: As soon as E9, developing pial vessels forming a vascular plexus surround the entire brain without following any obvious spatial or temporal gradient.
source: As soon as E9, developing pial vessels forming a vascular plexus surround the entire brain without following any obvious spatial or temporal gradient.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about early pial vessel development.

claim: The periventricular vessels develop in a ventral-to-dorsal gradient within the telencephalon.
source: By contrast, the periventricular vessels develop in a ventral-to-dorsal gradient within the telencephalon.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about periventricular vessel development patterns.

claim: Angiogenesis in the embryonic telencephalon is controlled by a set of region-specific transcription factors, from the ventral telencephalon such as Nkx2.1 and Dlx2, and from the dorsal telencephalon like Pax6 that are expressed in a subset of ECs.
source: Angiogenesis in the embryonic telencephalon, in addition to the extrinsic factors listed above, is also controlled by a set of region-specific transcription factors, from the ventral telencephalon such as Nkx2.1 and Dlx2, and from the dorsal telencephalon like Pax6 that are expressed in a subset of ECs (Vasudevan and Bhide, 2008; Vasudevan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on transcription factor control of telencephalic angiogenesis.

claim: The distinct spatial and temporal expression of these transcription factors has been shown to direct telencephalic vascular development.
source: The distinct spatial and temporal expression of these transcription factors has been shown to direct telencephalic vascular development.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about transcription factor roles in vascular development.

claim: Macrophages that lie in close proximity to the blood vessels have been known to act as angiogenic agents and have been implicated in blood vessel development during growth and repair.
source: Until now, macrophages that lie in close proximity to the blood vessels have been known to act as angiogenic agents and have been implicated in blood vessel development during growth and repair (Fantin et al., 2010; Newman and Hughes, 2012; Nucera et al., 2011; Outtz et al., 2011; Pollard, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on macrophage roles in angiogenesis.

claim: Early embryonic macrophages travel from the yolk sac, express Tie2 and the neuropilin 1 receptor, and are present at the time of brain vascularization.
source: In brain, early embryonic macrophages travel from the yolk sac, express Tie2 and the neuropilin 1 receptor, and are present at the time of brain vascularization.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about embryonic macrophage characteristics and timing.

claim: Macrophages were observed to localize at vessels junctions and interact with the endothelial tip cells, by forming bridges to align them and to prepare them for the later fusion.
source: They were observed to localize at vessels junctions and interact with the endothelial tip cells, by forming bridges to align them and to prepare them for the later fusion (Fantin et al., 2010; Nucera et al., 2011; Outtz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on macrophage-endothelial cell interactions.

claim: NG2+ glia or polydendrocytes constitute a population of cells that are different from neurons, mature oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglia.
source: NG2+ glia or polydendrocytes constitute a population of cells that are different from neurons, mature oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglia (Nishiyama et al., 2002; Nishiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature defining NG2+ glia as a distinct cell type.

claim: NG2+ glia express NG2 (Nerve/glial antigen 2 or CSPG for chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan) and Olig2 (Oligodendrocyte precursor bHLH transcription factor 2).
source: They express NG2 (Nerve/glial antigen 2 or CSPG for chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan) and Olig2 (Oligodendrocyte precursor bHLH transcription factor 2) but lack astrocytic markers namely GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) and GLAST (Astrocyte-specific glutamate and aspartate transporter).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NG2+ glia marker expression.

claim: NG2+ glia lack astrocytic markers namely GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) and GLAST (Astrocyte-specific glutamate and aspartate transporter).
source: They express NG2 (Nerve/glial antigen 2 or CSPG for chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan) and Olig2 (Oligodendrocyte precursor bHLH transcription factor 2) but lack astrocytic markers namely GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) and GLAST (Astrocyte-specific glutamate and aspartate transporter).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NG2+ glia marker expression.

claim: NG2+ glia display complex highly branched morphology and are uniformly distributed within the grey and white matter throughout all layers.
source: They display complex highly branched morphology and are uniformly distributed within the grey and white matter throughout all layers.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NG2+ glia morphology and distribution.

claim: NG2+ glia generate oligodendrocytes in vitro and have been considered since a long time as oligodendrocyte progenitor cells.
source: They generate oligodendrocytes in vitro and have been considered since a long time as oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (Polito and Reynolds, 2005; Nishiyama et al., 1996a, 1996b, 2009; Zhu et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on NG2+ glia differentiation potential.

claim: NG2+ glia have been shown to differentiate into neurons and protoplasmic astrocytes in the grey matter as well as in the white matter.
source: However, recently, NG2+ glia have also been shown to differentiate into neurons and protoplasmic astrocytes in the grey matter as well as in the white matter (Rivers et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2008b; Zhu et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on NG2+ glia differentiation potential.

claim: Electrophysiological studies indicate that NG2+ glia receive synaptic input from neurons.
source: Furthermore, electrophysiological studies indicate that NG2+ glia receive synaptic input from neurons, and like astroglia, probably participate to the neuronal network (Paukert and Bergles, 2006; Butt et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies on NG2+ glia.

claim: NG2+ glia, like astroglia, probably participate to the neuronal network.
source: Furthermore, electrophysiological studies indicate that NG2+ glia receive synaptic input from neurons, and like astroglia, probably participate to the neuronal network (Paukert and Bergles, 2006; Butt et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on inference from electrophysiological data and uses speculative language ('probably').

claim: NG2+ glia have been implicated in synaptic reorganization after cortical and spinal cord injury, but their precise role is still unknown.
source: NG2+ glia have also been implicated in synaptic reorganization after cortical and spinal cord injury, but their precise role is still unknown (Nishiyama, 2007; Nishiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on NG2+ glia in injury contexts.

claim: Between E12.5-to-E16.5, NG2+ glia were positioned within the marginal zone (MZ), the subplate, the intermediate zone (IZ) and the sub-ventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral cortical area, and in the septum (SEP) of the WT mice.
source: Between E12.5-to-E16.5, we observed that the NG2+ glia were positioned within the marginal zone (MZ), the subplate, the intermediate zone (IZ) and the sub-ventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral cortical area, and in the septum (SEP) of the WT mice (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: NG2+ glia populated the midline corticoseptal boundary (CSB) region at E12.5.
source: They populated the midline corticoseptal boundary (CSB) region at E12.5 (n=3) (Figure 1A), and the cingulate bundle (CI), the cingulate (CCi) and frontal (CFr) cortices at E14.5 (n=3) (Figure 1B and 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A with sample size n=3.

claim: NG2+ glia populated the cingulate bundle (CI), the cingulate (CCi) and frontal (CFr) cortices at E14.5.
source: They populated the midline corticoseptal boundary (CSB) region at E12.5 (n=3) (Figure 1A), and the cingulate bundle (CI), the cingulate (CCi) and frontal (CFr) cortices at E14.5 (n=3) (Figure 1B and 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 1B and 1C with sample size n=3.

claim: By E16.5, NG2+ glia were ubiquitously dispersed within the WT dorsal telencephalon.
source: By E16.5, NG2+ glia were ubiquitously dispersed within the WT dorsal telencephalon (n=3) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D with sample size n=3.

claim: In Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice, the YFP signal was detected in a majority of embryonic NG2+ glia of the dorsal telencephalon (at E18.5: 71.7 ± 14.6% in the corpus callosum (CC), 57 ± 3.8% in the CI and 69 ± 5.3% in the CCi; n=3).
source: In Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice, the YFP signal was detected in a majority of embryonic NG2+ glia of the dorsal telencephalon (at E18.5: 71.7 ± 14.6% in the corpus callosum (CC), 57 ± 3.8% in the CI and 69 ± 5.3% in the CCi; n=3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A with sample size n=3.

claim: The entire cell population visualized by the YFP signal at E16.5–E18.5 co-expressed NG2 and Olig2, two well-known markers for NG2 glia.
source: The entire cell population visualized by the YFP signal at E16.5–E18.5 co-expressed NG2 (n=3) and Olig2 (n=3), two well-known markers for NG2 glia, and also S100β (n=3) , considered as a marker for astrocytes and NG2+ glia (Cahoy et al., 2008; Honsa et al., 2012; Rivers et al., 2008) (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 2A-C with sample sizes n=3 for each marker.

claim: The entire cell population visualized by the YFP signal at E16.5–E18.5 co-expressed S100β, considered as a marker for astrocytes and NG2+ glia.
source: The entire cell population visualized by the YFP signal at E16.5–E18.5 co-expressed NG2 (n=3) and Olig2 (n=3), two well-known markers for NG2 glia, and also S100β (n=3) , considered as a marker for astrocytes and NG2+ glia (Cahoy et al., 2008; Honsa et al., 2012; Rivers et al., 2008) (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data and citations to literature on S100β expression.

claim: At E16.5-E18.5, YFP+ cells did not express the specific astrocytic markers GLAST and GFAP.
source: As expected, at same ages they did not express the specific astrocytic markers GLAST (n=3) and GFAP (n=3) (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 2D-E with sample sizes n=3 for each marker.

claim: In WT mice, PDGFR-β+ pericytes adjacent to the vessels were NG2+.
source: Although immunostaining showed that in WT mice, PDGFR-β+ pericytes adjacent to the vessels were NG2+ (Figure 3D), Cre-mediated recombination in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice did not occur properly in the pericytes.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice did not occur properly in the pericytes.
source: Although immunostaining showed that in WT mice, PDGFR-β+ pericytes adjacent to the vessels were NG2+ (Figure 3D), Cre-mediated recombination in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice did not occur properly in the pericytes.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of very few YFP+ pericytes in the subsequent analysis.

claim: Only very few PDGFR-β+ pericytes were labeled for the YFP in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP telencephalon.
source: As a result, although NG2 is expressed by pericytes (Levine and Nishiyama, 1996; Stallcup and Huang, 2008; Virgintino et al., 2007), we found only very few PDGFR-β+ pericytes labeled for the YFP in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP telencephalon (Figure 3B, n=3).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B with sample size n=3.

claim: Only 4.95 ± 1.54% of total PDGFR-β+ pericyte-population was co-labeled with YFP in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice.
source: Quantifications of the two populations: PDGFR-β+/YFP- pericytes and PDGFR-β+/YFP+ pericytes showed that only 4.95 ± 1.54% of total PDGFR-β+ pericyte-population was co-labeled with YFP (Figure 3G, n=10).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G with sample size n=10.

claim: Vast majority of the YFP signal in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP brains was present in NG2+ glia alone.
source: Thus, vast majority of the YFP signal in Cspg4-cre+/Rosa-EYFP brains was present in NG2+ glia alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the low percentage of YFP+ pericytes and high percentage of YFP+ NG2+ glia.

claim: Nkx2.1-regulated precursors have been previously shown in embryos to produce transient oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in addition to giving rise to GABAergic interneurons and astrocytes.
source: As Nkx2.1-regulated precursors have been previously shown in embryos to produce transient oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in addition to giving rise to GABAergic interneurons and astrocytes (Nery et al., 2001; Kessaris et al., 2006, Minocha et al., 2015), we decided to make use of the Nkx2.1-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice to look further at the subpallial origin, time of appearance and spatial arrangement of the embryonic NG2+ glia that ubiquitously occupied the dorsal telencephalon toward the end of embryonic development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Nkx2.1-derived cell types.

claim: Nkx2.1-derived precursors produced YFP+/NG2+ glia that colonized the cingulate cortical area and the midline.
source: Using our Nkx2.1-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice, our findings confirmed that Nkx2.1-derived precursors produced YFP+/NG2+ glia that colonized the cingulate cortical area and the midline (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, and confirmed by citation.

claim: The YFP signal was detected in all embryonic NG2+ glia of the dorsal telencephalon from E16.5 to E18.5 (100% colocalization in the CC, and the CCi at E16.5 and E18.5; n=5).
source: The YFP signal was detected in all embryonic NG2+ glia of the dorsal telencephalon from E16.5 to E18.5 (100% colocalization in the CC, and the CCi at E16.5 and E18.5; n=5) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F with sample size n=5.

claim: Nkx2.1-derived NG2+ glia expressed Olig2 and S100β.
source: Nkx2.1-derived NG2+ glia expressed Olig2 (n=5) and S100β (n=4) (Figure 2G–H), and lacked GLAST (n=4) or GFAP (n=3) expression (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 2G-H with sample sizes n=5 and n=4.

claim: Nkx2.1-derived NG2+ glia lacked GLAST or GFAP expression.
source: Nkx2.1-derived NG2+ glia expressed Olig2 (n=5) and S100β (n=4) (Figure 2G–H), and lacked GLAST (n=4) or GFAP (n=3) expression (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 2I-J with sample sizes n=4 and n=3.

claim: Subpallial domains are sites for early NG2+ glia genesis.
source: This further emphasized that subpallial domains are sites for early NG2+ glia genesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Nkx2.1-derived precursors produce NG2+ glia.

claim: The YFP+/Olig2+/NG2+ glia originating from Nkx2.1 domains were transient in nature and disappeared abruptly from the cortex around P8.
source: Furthermore, we followed the presence of these YFP+ /NG2+ glia after birth. We observed that the YFP+/Olig2+/NG2+ glia originating from Nkx2.1 domains were transient in nature and disappeared abruptly from the cortex around P8 (n=3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by postnatal immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with sample size n=3.

claim: The OPCs generated from the Nkx2.1-expressing precursors were shown to disappear around P10.
source: These results are coherent with previous studies, wherein the OPCs generated from the Nkx2.1-expressing precursors were shown to disappear around P10 (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on Nkx2.1-derived OPC fate.

claim: No YFP signal was detected in the ECs and the pericytes of the cerebral vasculature in Nkx2.1-cre+/Rosa-EYFP mice.
source: Interestingly, we never detected any YFP signal in the ECs and the pericytes of the cerebral vasculature (Figure 3A1 and 3C ; n=5).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 3A1 and 3C with sample size n=5.

claim: In embryos, NG2+ glia of the dorsal telencephalon are derived from Nkx2.1+ progenitors of the subpallium and transiently occupy the telencephalon.
source: These results altogether show that in embryos, NG2+ glia of the dorsal telencephalon are derived from Nkx2.1+ progenitors of the subpallium and transiently occupy the telencephalon.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental data.

claim: The disappearance of the Nkx2.1-derived NG2+ glia a few days after birth underlines their functional requirement for events occurring during embryonic and early postnatal period.
source: The disappearance of the Nkx2.1-derived NG2+ glia a few days after birth underlines their functional requirement for events occurring during embryonic and early postnatal period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal pattern of NG2+ glia presence and disappearance.

claim: At E14.5, the first pioneer NG2+ glia were observed in the CCi cortical plate (CP).
source: At E14.5 (n=3), the first pioneer NG2+ glia were observed in the CCi cortical plate (CP) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1 with sample size n=3.

claim: NG2+ glia occupied the CP at the same time as establishment of the blood vessel network and were seen to accompany it while growing and invading the dorsal telencephalon.
source: As such, they occupied the CP at the same time as establishment of the blood vessel network and were seen to accompany it while growing and invading the dorsal telencephalon.
evidence: This is based on observational data comparing the timing and spatial distribution of NG2+ glia and vessels.

claim: The NG2+ glia were present from E14.5-to-E16.5 throughout the dorsal telencephalon during the early phase of angiogenesis when vessels begin to extend, sprout, and form new branches.
source: The NG2+ glia were present from E14.5-to-E16.5 throughout the dorsal telencephalon during the early phase of angiogenesis when vessels begin to extend, sprout, and form new branches, as well as during the later phase from E16.5-to-E18.5 when branches fuse together or retract (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 1 and 2 across developmental stages.

claim: The NG2+ glia were present during the later phase from E16.5-to-E18.5 when branches fuse together or retract.
source: The NG2+ glia were present from E14.5-to-E16.5 throughout the dorsal telencephalon during the early phase of angiogenesis when vessels begin to extend, sprout, and form new branches, as well as during the later phase from E16.5-to-E18.5 when branches fuse together or retract (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 1 and 2 across developmental stages.

claim: NG2+ glia formed a complex cellular network around the cerebral vessels outlined by NG2, PECAM, Isolectin, or PDGFR-β labeling.
source: Interestingly, we observed that NG2+ glia formed a complex cellular network around the cerebral vessels outlined by NG2, PECAM, Isolectin, or PDGFR-β labeling (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: NG2+ glia were localized at sprouting tip cells or at branch fusion points, and also all along the vessel walls.
source: They were localized at sprouting tip cells or at branch fusion points, and also all along the vessel walls (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Several long and slender processes of the NG2+ glia appeared to wrap or tether to the vascular walls, possibly reflective of a functional interaction.
source: Several long and slender processes of the NG2+ glia appeared to wrap or tether to the vascular walls, possibly reflective of a functional interaction (Figure 1A3, 1B3, 1C3; open arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations from confocal imaging, with speculation about functional significance.

claim: The interactions between blood vessel network and NG2+ glia enhanced as embryonic age progressed.
source: The interactions between blood vessel network and NG2+ glia enhanced as embryonic age progressed (compare Figure 1A to 1D and 3D).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of images across developmental stages.

claim: NG2+ glia make multiple close contacts with different cortical blood vessels and created bridges between neighboring vessels.
source: A careful analysis using highly magnified three-dimensional (3D) confocal pictures combined with iso-surface representations revealed that NG2+ glia make multiple close contacts with different cortical blood vessels and created bridges between neighboring vessels (Figure 1D3).
evidence: This is supported by 3D confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1D3.

claim: The bridges are composed of several NG2+ glia that make connections via their entangled processes, and connect the neighbor vessels.
source: The bridges are composed of several NG2+ glia that make connections via their entangled processes, and connect the neighbor vessels (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: The strategic position of NG2+ glia between the blood vessels created an elaborate mesh-like structure, and reflected the possibility that NG2+ glia participated toward the vasculature connectivity.
source: The strategic position of NG2+ glia between the blood vessels created an elaborate mesh-like structure, and reflected the possibility that NG2+ glia participated toward the vasculature connectivity (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations with speculation about functional role.

claim: The location and timing of appearance of the transient NG2+ glia raise the possibility that they actively participate in the branching and refinement of the cerebral vasculature.
source: Therefore, the location and timing of appearance of the transient NG2+ glia raise the possibility that they actively participate in the branching and refinement of the cerebral vasculature.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed spatiotemporal correlation.

claim: Nkx2.1-cre+/Rosa-DTA mice allowed a selective ablation of Nkx2.1-derived post-mitotic cells without affecting Nkx2.1+ precursors because the diphtheria toxin expression under the control of Nkx2.1 promoter took several days.
source: Nkx2.1-cre+/Rosa-DTA mice allowed a selective ablation of Nkx2.1-derived post-mitotic cells without affecting Nkx2.1+ precursors because the diphtheria toxin expression under the control of Nkx2.1 promoter took several days (Minocha et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work characterizing this mouse model.

claim: Nkx2.1-regulated precursors are known to give rise to GABAergic interneurons and astrocytes.
